title: The circle around Kailash
hookLine: the pilgrimage around Mount Kailash, sacred to several traditions
carry: circle the holy, keeping it on your right

cards: Snow on a black pyramid of rock, alone above a high, bare plateau in western Tibet. Pilgrims don't walk up it. They walk around it.
A family walks together, the youngest riding on a father's shoulders.
A young man lies flat on the stony path, stretches his arms forward, marks the spot, stands, steps to the mark, and lies down again, measuring the whole circle with his body.

A group of pilgrims from India moves past, chanting a different name for the same mountain. Now and then, someone comes the other way, walking the circle in the opposite direction. The mountain is Kailash.

teach.b: First, a very old gesture. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is a way Buddhists show respect, and it goes back to the texts.
Again and again in the old discourses, someone who has listened to the Buddha rises, bows, and departs keeping him on the right.
So circling a stupa, a temple or a mountain clockwise carries that same bow forward, step by step. Second, the mountain.
For Tibetan Buddhists, Kailash is the home of a great meditation deity, and the circle around it, called a kora, is a pilgrimage they hold dear.

teach.h: THE KORA AND THE HIGH PASS.
teach.b: The path climbs to a high pass, where pilgrims hang prayer flags and some leave a small thing of their own, a bit of cloth, a lock of hair, as a sign of leaving the old life on the mountain. Third, the neighbors.
Kailash is not only a Buddhist mountain. Hindus honor it as the dwelling of Shiva. Jains revere it as a place of liberation.
Followers of Bon, the old religion of Tibet, hold it sacred too, and they walk the circle counterclockwise, by their own custom.

So people of several faiths pass one another on the same path, each for their own reasons, and nobody has to agree to share the trail. Fourth, why around and not up. Tradition holds the summit is not to be climbed.
The center stays untouched. The pilgrimage is the circle.

how: Tibetan Buddhist pilgrims walk the kora around Mount Kailash clockwise, some making full-body prostrations along the way, and Buddhists also circle stupas and temples clockwise as a sign of respect.

games.why: on the same path, people of several faiths go around the same peak by their own customs. the trail holds them all.

practice: Choose a center, a plant, a candle, a chair, an image that means something to you, and walk slowly around it clockwise, keeping it on your right, once or a few times; if you can't walk, trace the circle with your eyes.
Then stop facing the center and stay with it a moment. You don't need to reach it; you're circling it.

wordCard.voice: Around the mountain. The kora around Mount Kailash, walked by Buddhists and by people of several other faiths, circling a peak that tradition says is not to be climbed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali padakkhina: keeping to the right, the respectful way of circling something holy.

carryVoice: Your line: circle the holy, keeping it on your right. The center stays untouched, and many faiths share the trail. That's today, done.
